messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  (none)

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  (none)

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Marilyn Grant, a 72-year-old divorced city council member, had spent most of her life moving through the city with a practiced confidence, knowing the streets, the storefronts, and the faces that came with public service. That confidence was shaken one winter evening when she left a neighborhood meeting later than planned and walked to her car in a dim municipal lot behind the community center. A man approached from between two parked vehicles, grabbed her purse strap hard enough to wrench her shoulder, and shoved her back against the door. Marilyn remembered the smell of cigarette smoke on his coat, the shock of seeing how quickly a routine errand had turned dangerous, and the helplessness of standing still while he rifled through her bag and demanded her wallet and keys. Even after he ran off, she found herself staring at the empty lot, unable to gather her thoughts or trust that the silence meant she was safe.

In the weeks that followed, Marilyn found that ordinary moments in the city could carry that night back with them. The scrape of footsteps behind her in a hallway, a man in a hooded jacket near the council building, or the sight of a dark parking lot after a meeting would make her body tense before she had fully registered what she was seeing. She began checking over her shoulder more often, scanning entrances and cars with a vigilance that felt sensible to her, not exaggerated; after all, she was certain that the attack had shown her how quickly someone could be singled out when she let her guard down. In her own mind, the event had taught her that public spaces were no longer predictable, and that she had to stay alert if she wanted to avoid another humiliation or worse. What troubled her most was not only the memory of the mugging itself but the sense that it had changed the rules of ordinary life, making each trip to a meeting, a store, or her parking space feel like a test of whether she would be caught unaware again.

At work, Marilyn began altering the way she moved through her days. She asked staff to escort her to her car after evening sessions, parked closer to entrances when she could, and sometimes declined community events that would end after dark. She told herself these choices were practical for a woman her age, though privately she knew they were also a way of keeping the memory from returning with full force. Even so, the more she reorganized her routine around avoiding the places and times that reminded her of the assault, the smaller her world became. Colleagues noticed that she left meetings early and seemed distracted when discussion turned to neighborhood safety, and Marilyn found herself less willing to linger in the very public spaces that had once defined her role. She still wore the polished composure of an elected official, but beneath it she was always watching: for movement in the corner of her eye, for a stranger who stayed too close, for the instant when an ordinary evening might tip into danger.

Over time, that constant scanning wore her down. Marilyn slept lightly, replaying the shove and the demand for her purse whenever she heard a door slam outside her apartment or a car engine idle too long in the street. She had come to believe that being caught off guard was what had made her vulnerable, and that if she stayed attentive enough she might prevent another attack, yet the effort of staying vigilant left her exhausted and more irritable with her daughter and with staff. Her divorce had already taught her to manage on her own, and now she was reluctant to ask anyone to go places with her for fear of seeming weak or frightened. The city still mattered to her, and she disliked the way the mugging had started to narrow her life into routes she thought were safe and routes she no longer trusted.

By the time Marilyn sought help, the fear had not settled on its own. She was still showing up for council duties, but she was doing so with a strained, watchful energy that left little room for ease. She came to therapy after realizing that the city she served was becoming, in her mind, a place full of threats she could not afford to ignore, and that her efforts to stay safe were no longer giving her the freedom they once promised. What she hoped for was simple but hard won: to be able to leave a meeting, cross a parking lot, and return home without feeling as though she had to brace for an attack at every turn.
